1065.title: Two ways of speaking
1065.hook: conventional truth (people, tables) and ultimate truth (momentary mind and matter)
1065.howItsDone: Theravada teachers use the two truths, conventional and ultimate, to explain how the Buddha could speak of persons while teaching not-self, and the chariot of Nagasena is a common teaching story.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Buddha taught the higher teaching to his mother among the gods. Your line: a gift to his mother.

Someone in the kitchen asks you to grab the chair by the window. Nobody answers: which collection of wooden parts, held together by glue and screws, do you mean? And yet the second answer isn't wrong. Two days ago there was a puzzle on the shelf: a book that takes people apart into moments, right next to a book that sorts kinds of people. Today, the key: two ways of speaking, both of them true.
screen: `GRAB THE CHAIR BY THE WINDOW.` → `WHICH COLLECTION OF PARTS?` → `BOTH ANSWERS, TRUE.`

segments.voice: The commentaries name them. Conventional truth is the way the world talks: people, tables, chairs, a mother, a son. Ultimate truth is the way the Abhidhamma talks: moments of mind and bits of matter, arising and passing away. First, the old picture. In the Questions of King Milinda, a monk named Nagasena asks the king how he came. By chariot. Is the pole the chariot? No. The wheels, the axle, the frame, the seat? No, no, no. Is there a chariot apart from all those? No. So where is the chariot? The king works it out: chariot is a name used for all those parts put together. And Nagasena says his own name works the same way. Second, the Buddha's own habit. In a discourse in the Digha Nikaya, after a long talk about the self, he says, in paraphrase, that words like these are the world's ordinary expressions, and he uses them without being misled by them. He said I and you, and told stories about kings and farmers. Third, the point that makes the puzzle go away. Conventional doesn't mean false. It means agreed on, useful, how a life gets lived. You can't keep a promise to a stream of mind-moments; you keep it to your sister. That's why the book of persons belongs in the basket. Fourth, why the second way matters. Speaking only the first way, it's easy to think there's a solid someone in there, the same yesterday and tomorrow. The second way lets a person see the parts, so anger or pride is seen as weather passing through, not as who they are.
screen: `CONVENTIONAL AND ULTIMATE.` · `WHERE IS THE CHARIOT?` · `HE SAID I, WITHOUT BEING MISLED.` · then, large: `CONVENTIONAL DOESN'T MEAN FALSE.`

segments.voice: If you'd like, choose one thing near you, a cup, say, and describe it the ordinary way: my cup, the blue one, a gift. Then slowly the other way: a shape seen, a color, a hardness, a thought that says mine. Then turn it on yourself, me, sitting here, and then breath moving, a pressure where the body meets the seat, sounds arriving, and let both be true.
Two ways of speaking. Conventional truth, people and tables, and ultimate truth, moments of mind and matter, each true in its own way. Today's word.
Your line: two ways of speaking. The chariot and its parts, each true in its own way. See you tomorrow.

1066.title: Four realities
1066.hook: consciousness, mental factors, matter, and nibbana
1066.howItsDone: Students of the Abhidhamma in Theravada communities learn the four ultimate realities, consciousness, mental factors, matter and nibbana, as the opening frame of the manuals they study.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a chair, a chariot, and the key to a puzzle: conventional truth and ultimate truth. Your line: two ways of speaking.

How many things are in the room you're sitting in? Count the ordinary way and you'll never finish: a lamp, a cable, a sock under the couch, a spider in the corner, the smell of coffee, a worry about Thursday. The Abhidhamma counts the ultimate way, and its answer is short. However crowded the room, however crowded the mind, everything real in that sense falls into four kinds. Four drawers. Today they open.
screen: `HOW MANY THINGS IN THIS ROOM?` → `THE ORDINARY COUNT NEVER ENDS.` → `FOUR DRAWERS.`

segments.voice: Today's word is paramattha, usually put into English as ultimate, or the highest sense: what the Abhidhamma counts as real when everything is taken apart, the bottom of the analysis, where taking apart stops. The manuals name four. The first drawer is citta, consciousness: the bare knowing of something. Seeing a color, hearing a sound, knowing a thought. The second is cetasika, the mental factors that come along with each moment of knowing and color it: feeling pleasant or unpleasant, attention, greed, kindness, doubt. The two always arrive together, the way light and the color of a stained glass window arrive together. The third is rupa, matter: the body, and the physical world the senses meet. Hardness, warmth, movement, color, sound. Everything in those three drawers arises from conditions, stays a moment, and passes away. Nothing in them lasts. The fourth drawer is different. It's nibbana, the ending of craving that this path has met before. The manuals list it as the one reality not made from conditions. It doesn't arise and doesn't pass away. In a discourse in the Udana, the Buddha speaks, in paraphrase, of something unborn and unmade, and says that if there weren't, there'd be no escape from what is born and made. Notice what isn't in any drawer. No lamp. No sock. And no self, sitting behind it all as the owner. A person, in the ultimate way of speaking, is the first three drawers, moving fast, and the fourth is what the whole path points toward.
screen: `CITTA: THE KNOWING.` · `CETASIKA: WHAT COLORS IT.` · `RUPA: MATTER.` · then, large: `NIBBANA: UNMADE.`

segments.voice: If you'd like, wait for one moment to stand out, a sound, an itch, a thought about later, and sort it gently: the knowing of it is the first drawer; the flavor that came with it, liking, impatience, curiosity, is the second; the sound or the skin is the third. The fourth you can't put a moment into, so let it rest in the background as what the sorting is for. Don't worry about getting it right; just sort the next moment the same way.

1067.title: Moments of mind
1067.hook: consciousness as a stream of tiny moments, each arising and passing
1067.howItsDone: In Theravada insight meditation, practitioners watch thoughts, sounds and sensations arise and pass, and teachers often explain what they see using the Abhidhamma's account of mind as a stream of moments.

segments.voice: Yesterday, four drawers: consciousness, mental factors, matter, and nibbana. Your line: four realities.

A flip book is a small stack of paper with a drawing in the corner of every page. Each drawing is still: a stick figure with one leg forward, then the leg a little further, then further. Riffle the stack with your thumb, and the figure runs. It looks like one smooth motion, but there's no running on any single page. The running happens in the flipping. Today the first drawer opens, and the Abhidhamma says the mind is a little like that flip book.
screen: `A DRAWING ON EVERY PAGE.` → `RIFFLE IT, AND IT RUNS.` → `NO RUNNING ON ANY ONE PAGE.`

segments.voice: Today's word is citta, usually put into English as mind, or consciousness: the knowing of something. First, the Abhidhamma's claim. Mind isn't one steady light left on all day. It's a stream of tiny moments of knowing, each arising, staying for an instant, and passing away, followed by the next. The commentaries give each moment three phases: arising, standing, dissolving. Second, the seed of this in the suttas. In the Samyutta Nikaya, the Buddha pictures a monkey moving through a forest: it grabs a branch, lets it go, grabs another. In paraphrase, he says what we call mind is like that: by day and by night, it arises as one thing and ceases as another. And in the Anguttara Nikaya, he says he can't point to anything that changes as quickly as the mind. Third, why it matters. If mind is one steady thing, a bad mood can seem like a fact about who someone is. If mind is moments, the bad mood is a run of pages in the flip book, and the next page isn't drawn yet. The Dhammapada opens, in Max Müller's translation, with a line some readers hear alongside this: "All that we are is the result of what we have thought: it is founded on our thoughts, it is made up of our thoughts." Fourth, the quiet surprise. Watched closely, the stream doesn't need a watcher behind it. The knowing of an itch is one moment; the knowing that you noticed it is the next. There's riffling, and figures running, and no one sitting inside the book.
screen: `ONE MOMENT OF KNOWING AT A TIME.` · `THE MONKEY IN THE FOREST.` · `THE NEXT PAGE ISN'T DRAWN YET.` · then, large: `NO ONE INSIDE THE BOOK.`

segments.voice: If you'd like, watch the mind the way you'd watch a road from a window, not chasing thoughts and not pushing them away: a thought appears and goes, then a sound, a memory, a plan for dinner. If you get carried off on one, that's the monkey grabbing a branch; notice that too, and come back to watching. You're not trying to stop the flicker, only to see that it flickers.

Your line: moment by moment. A mood is a run of pages, not the whole book. Same time tomorrow.

1068.title: How seeing happens
1068.hook: a sense object strikes, the mind turns, sees, receives, judges, responds: a process in a flash
1068.howItsDone: Theravada teachers who use the Abhidhamma describe each perception as a quick series of mind-moments, and in insight meditation practitioners note seeing, hearing and reacting as separate events.

segments.voice: Yesterday, citta: mind as a flip book of tiny moments, and a monkey swinging from branch to branch. Your line: moment by moment.

Crash. In the next room, something has fallen off a shelf. Before any decision gets made, the head has already turned. Then a split second of just looking: a scatter of white on the floor. Then: a mug. Then: the blue one, the good one. And fast behind it, a feeling with a voice: oh no, or who left that there, or it's fine, it was chipped anyway. It all seems to happen at once. The Abhidhamma slows it down, frame by frame, and finds a sequence with an order to it.
screen: `CRASH, IN THE NEXT ROOM.` → `THE HEAD HAS ALREADY TURNED.` → `FRAME BY FRAME.`

segments.voice: The manuals call this a process, a road the mind travels. First, the stream at rest. Between experiences, the mind runs along quietly, a kind of background current. Then an object strikes: a sight hits the eye, a sound hits the ear, and the quiet current shivers and is cut. Second, the mind turns. One moment does nothing but turn toward the door the object came in by, the eye or the ear. That's the head turning before anyone decided anything. Third, seeing itself. Not a mug yet, not the blue one: color and shape, bare. Fourth, a quick run of sorting moments: the sight is received, then examined, then settled on: it's a mug. Only then comes the response. The manuals call it javana, a word that means something like running, or impulse. This is where the mind likes, dislikes, grieves, shrugs, and this, the manuals say, is where kamma is made. Everything before it simply happened. In a discourse in the Udana, the Buddha gives a wandering seeker named Bahiya a very short teaching. In paraphrase: in the seen, let there be only the seen; in the heard, only the heard. The Abhidhamma's road is a map of why that's hard, and where it can be done. The gap where something can change is at the response: not by refusing to see the broken mug, but by catching the moment the mind starts running, and noticing it run.
screen: `THE QUIET CURRENT IS STRUCK.` · `THE MIND TURNS.` · `JUST SEEING.` · then, large: `THE RESPONSE: WHERE KAMMA IS MADE.`

segments.voice: If you'd like, rest your eyes low, then let them lift to one thing in front of you, and before you name it, stay with just the seeing for a breath: color, edges, light. Then let the naming come, a plant, a window, a shoe, and watch for the response, the faint like, or dislike, or nothing much. Close your eyes, open them on something new, and walk the road again: turn, see, name, respond.
How seeing happens. A process in a flash: the object strikes, the mind turns, sees, receives, sorts, and then responds. Today's word.
Your line: seeing is a process. Most of the road arrives on its own; the response is the open step. Until tomorrow.

1069.title: The mango simile
1069.hook: a man asleep under a tree, woken by a falling mango, picks it up, smells it, eats it: the steps of one perception (a commentary simile)
1069.howItsDone: Teachers of the Abhidhamma in Theravada communities use the mango simile to explain the stages of a single perception, and some insight meditation retreats use slow, mindful eating as an exercise.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a mug crashed in the next room, and the Abhidhamma slowed the moment down: turn, see, sort, respond. Your line: seeing is a process.

Hot afternoon. A man lies asleep at the foot of a mango tree, his head covered with a cloth. The leaves are still. Then a ripe mango lets go of its branch, drops, and lands with a thump right by his ear. That's the whole setup. It isn't from the suttas. It's a simile from the commentaries, the teachers who came after and tried to make the Abhidhamma's road easy to remember. Yesterday's road was a diagram. Today it gets a body, a tree, and a piece of fruit.
screen: `ASLEEP UNDER A MANGO TREE.` → `A THUMP BY HIS EAR.` → `A DIAGRAM GETS A BODY.`

segments.voice: Follow the man, and you're following yesterday's road. First, sleep. His sleep is the quiet current of the mind, running along with nothing in particular in it. The falling mango is the object striking, and the thump that wakes him is the current being cut. Second, he wakes and turns. He pulls the cloth off his head and looks around: the mind turning toward the door the object came in by. He sees the mango: just seeing. Third, the sorting. He picks it up: receiving. He squeezes it a little: examining. He smells it and decides, ripe: the settling, the moment that says, this is a mango, a good one. Fourth, the eating. He eats it, and enjoys it. In the simile, the eating is the response, javana, where the mind acts and kamma is made. Then he swallows the last of the taste, lies back down, and falls asleep again, until the next mango. Notice what he chose and what he didn't. He didn't choose the mango falling, or waking, or seeing it. Most of the simile happens to him. Only at the eating does he do something, and even then it's a very ordinary thing. That's the point the teachers wanted remembered. Life drops mangoes: sounds, sights, a message, a smell from someone's kitchen. Most of the road is automatic. The place to look is the eating: what the mind does with what has fallen.

segments.voice: If you have a piece of fruit nearby, a grape, a slice of apple, a raisin, hold it; if not, use a sip of water or tea. Look at it, feel its weight and skin, smell it, and notice when the mind says ripe, good, I want this. Then eat it slowly, watch the liking happen, and rest in the quiet after, the way the man lies back down under his tree.

1070.title: Kinds of consciousness
1070.hook: the manuals count 89 types of consciousness; the point is to see how varied mind is
1070.howItsDone: Students of the Abhidhamma in Theravada communities learn the manual's list of the kinds of consciousness, often with charts, and teachers use it to help meditators recognize the many states of mind they meet.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a man asleep under a tree, a mango thumping down by his ear, and the eating where he finally acts. Your line: the mango falls.

At the paint store there's a wall of little color cards, and a whole stretch of it is white. Eggshell. Linen. Chalk. Bone. Cloud. Held up one by one, they all look like white. Laid side by side, they're plainly different, warm and cool, bright and dull, and a person who works with paint can tell them apart at a glance. The mind, from the inside, can seem a bit like plain white: just me, thinking. The Abhidhamma holds up the cards side by side.
screen: `A WALL OF WHITES.` → `SIDE BY SIDE, ALL DIFFERENT.` → `THE MIND, CARD BY CARD.`

segments.voice: A manual this path has been leaning on, the Abhidhammattha Sangaha, counts the kinds of consciousness, citta, and its count is eighty-nine. It isn't really meant as a test. It's a way of showing how varied mind is. First, it sorts by where a moment belongs. Some belong to ordinary life in the world of the senses: seeing a bus, wanting a sandwich. Some belong to deep meditation, states the texts describe as calm and bright. And some belong to the moments of awakening itself. Second, it sorts by roots. Some moments are rooted in greed, some in aversion, some in confusion; others in their opposites: generosity, kindness, understanding. Third, it notices the feeling that comes along: pleasure, a flat, neutral tone, or displeasure. Fourth, a smaller detail. The manual separates moments that arise on their own from moments that needed a push, from yourself or from someone else. So a kind act done spontaneously and the same act done after a friend nudged you count as two different kinds of mind. Neither is thrown out. The nudged kindness is still kindness, but they're not the same card. What's the use of all this sorting on an ordinary Tuesday? It loosens a habit. It's easy to say I'm an anxious person, or I'm a generous person, as if the mind were one color. Card by card, the mind is many: anxious moments, generous moments, bored moments, tender moments, each arising and passing, and none of them the whole wall.

1071.title: Four families
1071.hook: wholesome, unwholesome, resultant and functional states of mind
1071.howItsDone: Abhidhamma students in Theravada communities learn to classify each kind of consciousness as wholesome, unwholesome, resultant or functional, and teachers use the scheme to show where kamma is made.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a wall of white paint cards, and a manual that counts eighty-nine kinds of mind. Your line: mind is many. Today the week closes.

All week, the mind has been on the bench, taken apart piece by piece, the way a watchmaker lays out a watch. Today, one more way of sorting, and it's the one that ties the week together. Every moment of mind, the Abhidhamma says, belongs to one of four families. Two of them are familiar. The other two are where it gets interesting.
screen: `THE MIND, ON THE BENCH ALL WEEK.` → `ONE MORE WAY OF SORTING.` → `FOUR FAMILIES.`

segments.voice: First, the wholesome family, kusala. The commentaries give the word several shades: healthy, blameless, skillful, and bringing good results. A wholesome moment is rooted in generosity, kindness, or understanding. Second, the unwholesome family, akusala: moments rooted in greed, aversion, or confusion. These first two are the families that act. They're the eating under the mango tree, where kamma is made. Third, the resultant family, vipaka: the ripening of earlier actions. And here's the surprise. The manuals count bare seeing, hearing, smelling and tasting as resultant. When a rude message lands on your phone, the simple seeing of the words isn't a deed at all. It's a result, arriving. The acting comes after, in what the mind does with it. Fourth, the functional family, kiriya. These moments do a job and leave no seed behind. The moment that turns the mind toward the crash in the next room is functional: it just turns. And the manuals say this about the awakened. When an arahant, one who has fully woken up, acts with kindness, the moment is counted as functional. It does its work, it helps, and it plants nothing more. So the four families aren't a scorecard for sorting yourself into good or bad. They're a map of where the choosing happens. Results arrive. Functional moments do their job. And in between, at the response, a moment comes out wholesome or unwholesome: the narrow place where something can change.
screen: `KUSALA: WHOLESOME.` · `AKUSALA: UNWHOLESOME.` · `VIPAKA: RESULTS, ARRIVING.` · then, large: `KIRIYA: IT DOES ITS JOB, AND NO MORE.`

segments.voice: If you'd like, sit and wait until something arrives, a sound, a memory, an itch, and let it arrive; that's a result. Then watch what the mind does next, and if anything kind, patient, generous or clear turns up, even faintly, just see it. There's no need to make one happen; noticing one is the practice.
Four families. Wholesome, unwholesome, resultant and functional: four ways the Abhidhamma sorts every moment of mind. Today's word.
